Formats#

Formats represent tensors and operators as chains of PyTorch cores. Construct one from its cores, then evaluate entries, contract it, or use its numerical operations. They do not create TensorKrowch graph nodes; graph-based models remain available through models.

import torch
import tensorkrowch as tk

f = tk.formats
cores = [torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 3, dtype=torch.float64)]
tt = f.TT(cores)
samples = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2], [2, 0, 1]])
values = tt.evaluate(samples)
tensor = tt.contract_dense()

If the cores are not yet known, use a decomposition to compute them from tensor values or a function. Decomposition results inherit the corresponding numerical format.

TensorFormat defines the common numerical interface. TensorFormat1D adds chain operations shared by these formats. The Format API reference contains all classes and their detailed method contracts.

Tensor trains and tensor rings#

Tensor trains#

A TT has open boundaries. An interior core has shape (left_rank, input_dimension, right_rank). The first core omits its unit left bond, and the last omits its unit right bond. A one-site TT is a vector. The neighboring bond dimensions must agree.

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64),
])
dimensions = tt.in_dim
ranks = tt.rank
tensor = tt.contract_dense()

This represents a tensor of shape (3, 4, 5) using internal ranks [2, 2]. cores contains its stored tensors; in_dim describes the physical dimensions and n_sites counts the sites.

Tensor rings#

A TR retains both virtual axes on every core, including the first and last. The last core’s right bond connects to the first core’s left bond. Every core therefore has shape (left_rank, input_dimension, right_rank).

tr = f.TR([
    torch.randn(2, 3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
])
tensor = tr.contract_dense()
open_chain = tr.to_tt()

The dense tensor again has shape (3, 4, 5). TR ranks include the cyclic bond. to_tt carries that closing index through the open chain, preserving values but potentially increasing TT ranks. Conversely, TT.to_tr adds a unit-rank closing bond; finding a compact nontrivial ring is the role of TT2TR.

Evaluation and numerical operations#

Evaluating selected entries#

evaluate accepts integer configurations or physical feature vectors. Integer inputs select entries; feature vectors contract with each site’s physical axis. A tensor groups inputs on the site axis; a sequence can provide differently sized feature vectors at different sites.

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 3, dtype=torch.float64),
])
indices = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2], [2, 0, 1]])
features = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(indices, num_classes=3).to(tt.dtype)
indexed_values = tt.evaluate(indices)
embedded_values = tt.evaluate(features)
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_values, embedded_values)

Use in_sites to evaluate only some variables or change their input order. Configuration columns follow the order of that selection. Remaining axes are returned in their original chain order, after the data and structural batch axes:

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64),
])
# Columns select site 2 and then site 0; site 1 stays open.
inputs = torch.tensor([[4, 0], [1, 2]])
fibers = tt.evaluate(inputs, in_sites=(2, 0))

Here fibers has shape (2, 4). A constructor’s in_sites sets the default selection; an evaluation call can override it. TR uses the same input conventions. contract_dense instead materializes every physical axis.

Formats can store leading structural batches through the constructor’s n_batches argument. These are separate from the data batches supplied when evaluating a format; see the API shapes for their ordering.

Arithmetic and errors#

Arithmetic works directly on cores without constructing the full tensor. For compatible formats, use + for addition, hadamard for entrywise products, and norm for the Frobenius norm. @ performs vector/operator products according to row/column orientation. T transposes without conjugation; H takes the adjoint.

tt = f.TT([torch.eye(3, dtype=torch.float64),
           torch.eye(3, dtype=torch.float64)])
summed = tt + tt
entrywise = tt.hadamard(tt)
squared_norm = tt.H @ tt
distance = tt.distance(summed)

These operations can increase ranks. Compression is an explicit subsequent step. TT.error() and its ring counterpart compare a format with a target function on supplied configurations and return a SampleError. clone, detach and to provide copying, autograd and device/dtype operations; their API documents when storage is shared.

Cores, bonds and gauges#

Optional bonds hold diagonal factors between neighboring cores. Pass the factor sequence to the constructor; the format creates its own BondFactors1D container. format.cores and format.bonds together represent the tensor, so stored factors must be included in contractions.

cores = [torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64)]
factors = [torch.tensor([1., 0.5], dtype=torch.float64),
           torch.tensor([1., 0.25], dtype=torch.float64)]
tt = f.TT(cores, bonds=factors)
absorbed = tt.clone().materialize_bonds(orth_center=1)
torch.testing.assert_close(tt.contract_dense(), absorbed.contract_dense())

TensorFormat1D.materialize_bonds() absorbs these factors into cores. It acts in place; clone first to retain the original representation. TR and matrix formats use the same factor container with their corresponding bond layout.

Canonical forms#

TT.canonicalize performs QR/RQ sweeps without truncation and moves the orthogonality center to the requested site. On an open chain, the cores to its left and right become isometric in the corresponding directions.

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64),
])
canonical = tt.clone().canonicalize(orth_center=1)
vidal = tt.clone().canonicalize_vidal(mode='explicit')
spectra = vidal.bonds.spectra

For TT and TTM, TT.canonicalize_vidal() stores a VidalGauge. Its spectra retain the Schmidt values and its powers describe how those values are distributed between neighboring cores. Modes "explicit", "implicit", "inverse", "left" and "right" select common distributions. The method preserves the tensor and does not truncate ranks. The API explains inverse_positions and the cutoff for inverse factors.

For a ring, canonicalize sets a local gauge relative to the stored cut; it is not a global Schmidt canonical form. To balance cyclic core gauges, use TR.canonicalize_minimal():

tr = f.TR([
    torch.randn(2, 3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
])
balanced, info = tr.clone().canonicalize_minimal(
    max_iter=20, return_info=True)

This optimization preserves the tensor and returns optional MinimalCanonicalInfo diagnostics. It need not reach its balance tolerance within a fixed iteration budget. Open-chain TT.canonicalize_minimal() uses implicit Vidal form without iterative optimization.

For custom gauge analysis, TensorRingOrbit exposes the ring’s gauge objective and bond Gram matrices; GaugeOrbit provides the general core-and-bond interface. Ordinary canonicalization does not require creating these objects yourself.

Compression and blocking#

TT.rounding and TR.rounding compress bond dimensions in place. Use rank for a shared rank cap, or singular-value truncation criteria such as rtol. rtol limits relative discarded squared mass locally; rel_error instead requests a global relative Frobenius error budget.

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64),
])
rounded, info = tt.clone().rounding(rank=1, return_info=True)
measured_error = tt.distance(rounded) / tt.norm()
error_bound = info.error_bound

RoundingInfo records the retained ranks and truncation information. Its error bound is distinct from the measured reconstruction error. Stricter rank caps or other simultaneous criteria may prevent the requested error budget from being met. Ring rounding includes the cyclic bond but does not guarantee minimal TR ranks.

To solve problems on larger local blocks, TensorFormat1D.block() contracts consecutive groups into effective sites. It returns a BlockLayout describing how to restore the original dimensions:

tt = f.TT([
    torch.randn(3, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    torch.randn(2, 5, dtype=torch.float64),
])
blocked = tt.clone()
layout = blocked.block([2, 1])
restored = blocked.unblock(layout)
torch.testing.assert_close(restored.contract_dense(), tt.contract_dense())

Both operations modify the format. split_block() provides the local splitting operation directly and returns a SplitBlock. For Quantics, convert to an ordinary format before grouping arbitrary digit sites, so the coordinate layout is not implicitly changed.

Matrix formats#

TTM and TRM attach an input and output physical axis to every site. Their cores use the order (left_rank, input_dimension, right_rank, output_dimension), omitting the first and last unit bonds for TTM. For example, a product identity operator on dimensions (2, 3) is:

matrix = f.TTM([
    torch.eye(2, dtype=torch.float64).reshape(2, 1, 2),
    torch.eye(3, dtype=torch.float64).reshape(1, 3, 3),
])
vector = f.TT([torch.randn(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
               torch.randn(2, 3, dtype=torch.float64)])
applied = matrix.apply(vector)
product = matrix @ vector
torch.testing.assert_close(
    applied.contract_dense(), vector.contract_dense())
torch.testing.assert_close(
    product.contract_dense(), vector.contract_dense())

For a TRM, keep both bond axes on every core and match the closing bond. in_dim and out_dim describe the input/output dimensions. Matrix contract_dense returns interleaved physical axes (in_0, out_0, in_1, out_1, ...).

TTM.evaluate() and TRM.evaluate() accept separate in_data and out_data. Their columns follow in_sites and out_sites; unselected axes are returned in chain order, with input-side axes before output-side axes. Both selections default to all sites. apply contracts every input physical dimension and returns an output format, rather than selected matrix entries. Transpose and adjoint retain the concrete matrix format.

Quantics formats#

Quantics splits each original coordinate index into several digit sites. QTT and QTR use the TT/TR core layouts, with digit dimensions as their physical dimensions. Construct them from cores and a grid specification:

cores = [torch.randn(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64)]
qtt = f.QTT(cores, n_coordinates=1, base=2, level=3,
            domain=torch.tensor([0., 1.], dtype=torch.float64))
coordinates = torch.tensor([[0.], [0.25], [0.75]], dtype=torch.float64)
values = qtt.evaluate_coordinates(coordinates)
grid_tensor = qtt.contract_dense_grid_axes()

The three binary sites represent eight grid points for one coordinate. contract_dense retains one axis per digit site, while contract_dense_grid_axes combines them into one axis per coordinate. evaluate_coordinates quantizes using the coordinate map; it does not interpolate between grid values.

A QTR uses three-axis cores including the cyclic bond. QTTM and QTRM use matrix cores and separate input/output coordinate descriptions through their in_* and out_* arguments. The two sides can have different numbers of coordinates and digit sites, selected by in_sites and out_sites.

Layouts and coordinate maps#

The convenience arguments create these objects automatically:

  • base, level and domain create a QuantizedLayout and an AffineCoordinateMap. Defaults use interleaved digit sites, coarse-to-fine digit order and a left-offset grid.

  • grid_coordinates replaces domain with an ExplicitGridMap. Each coordinate grid must contain base ** level points.

  • Explicit layout and coordinate_map objects allow other schedules and coordinate transformations.

The available coordinate objects are:

Object

Role

QuantizedLayout

Convert integer grid indices to digits and choose their site order.

AffineCoordinateMap

Map coordinates to an affine grid over a domain.

ExplicitGridMap

Map coordinates to explicitly supplied grid points.

FunctionalCoordinateMap

Apply user-defined forward and optional inverse coordinate functions.

CoordinateMap

Common interface for coordinate/grid-index conversion.

For example, two coordinates can use different digit counts:

layout = f.QuantizedLayout(
    n_coordinates=2, base=2, level=(2, 1), ordering='grouped')
coordinate_map = f.AffineCoordinateMap(
    domain=torch.tensor([[0., 1.], [-1., 1.]], dtype=torch.float64),
    grid_size=layout.grid_size)
cores = [torch.randn(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
         torch.randn(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64)]
qtt = f.QTT(cores, n_coordinates=2, layout=layout,
            coordinate_map=coordinate_map)
coordinates = torch.tensor([[0., -1.], [0.5, 0.]], dtype=torch.float64)
indices = coordinate_map.to_indices(coordinates)
digits = layout.encode_indices(indices)
values = qtt.evaluate_coordinates(coordinates)
torch.testing.assert_close(values, qtt.evaluate_indices(indices))
torch.testing.assert_close(values, qtt.evaluate_digits(digits))

The evaluation path is coordinate map, integer grid indices, layout encoding, then digit-core contraction. evaluate_indices starts at grid indices; evaluate_digits starts at digits. The map’s grid_size must agree with the layout. QuantizedLayout.decode_digits and CoordinateMap.from_indices provide the reverse conversions.

For matrix variants, pass in_layout, out_layout, in_coordinate_map and out_coordinate_map independently. Their API explains the coordinate and digit shapes on each side.

Models and decomposition results#

Use TT.to_mps() / TR.to_mps() to create graph-based MPS models, and TTM.to_mpo() / TRM.to_mpo() for MPO models. Open and cyclic formats retain their corresponding boundary conditions. parameterized controls whether the new model uses trainable nodes.

TT.from_mps() and TTM.from_mpo(), and their cyclic counterparts, convert compatible models back to formats. Conversions handle stored bond factors; callers do not need to absorb them manually first.

Decompositions return numerical formats enriched with fit metrics and metadata. Use result.to_format() to keep the numerical representation alone. Source adapters provide the opposite direction: FormatSource lets algorithms evaluate an existing format without turning it into a graph model.
